draft.title: Psychological skills and sleep
card: Psychological skills are strategies an athlete can learn and practise, in the same way as a physical skill. They support performance and enjoyment of sport.
Confidence
belief in your ability to do a task. Positive self-talk, such as telling yourself "I have trained for this", and picturing a skill done well (imagery) can build it.
Focus
keeping attention on what matters now and ignoring distractions. A short routine, such as the same steps before a free throw, or a cue word can help bring attention back.
Sleep
the body recovers and the brain rests during sleep. Regular sleep and wake times, a dark and quiet room, and less screen use before bed can improve sleep quality.
draft.remember: Confidence, focus and sleep can all be improved with strategies that are practised.

a.q: Before each penalty kick, Ravi takes a deep breath and says the cue word "target". Which skill is he mainly using this routine for?
opts: Focus, to keep attention on the task
Confidence, to recover from past goals
Sleep, to rest the brain before play
Recovery, to repair muscle after play
a.why: A routine and a cue word help an athlete keep attention on the task and ignore distractions, which is focus. Confidence is tempting, but the cue word is not about belief in ability. It points attention at the kick.
a.clue: What is the cue word helping Ravi attend to?

b.q: Priya, a netballer in Geelong, scrolls on her phone in bed until midnight before morning games and feels flat. Which change would best improve her sleep?
opts: Put the phone away before bed and keep a set bedtime
Use positive self-talk during the warm-up on game day
Picture a perfect shooting routine while in bed
Use a cue word to stay focused during the third quarter
b.why: Less screen use before bed and regular sleep times are strategies for better sleep. Self-talk, imagery and cue words are psychological skills for confidence and focus, and they do not fix a late bedtime.
b.clue: Which option changes what happens before and during sleep?

a.best: Focus, to keep attention on the task

b.best: Put the phone away before bed and keep a set bedtime

problems.detail: The distractor 'Confidence, to recover from past goals' is unclear. It does not say whether the goals were scored, conceded or missed, or what 'recover' means here. The other two distractors (recovery, sleep) plainly do not fit a pre-kick cue word, so the question is very easy for Year 11.

a.q: When the crowd gets loud before a penalty kick, Ravi takes a deep breath and says the cue word "target". What is the cue word mainly doing?
opts: Bringing his attention back to the kick
Building his belief that he can score
Reminding him of the training he has done
Picturing the ball hitting the back of the net
a.why: A cue word helps an athlete bring attention back to the task and ignore distractions such as crowd noise, which is focus. Building belief is tempting, but that is confidence, built by self-talk such as "I have trained for this". The word "target" points his attention at the kick rather than stating belief in his ability.
a.clue: Think about what the crowd noise is pulling away from Ravi.
